strengths: Significance: Sharper dimension dependence and high-probability guarantees for widely used adaptive optimizers are worthwhile theoretical goals; a useful contribution need not introduce a new algorithm.
Technical approach: The auxiliary iterate and lagged-preconditioner decomposition address the relevant difficulties of momentum and dependence between stochastic gradients and adaptive scaling.

Presentation and reproducibility: Explicit pseudocode, assumptions, theorem constants, and extensive proof appendices facilitate independent checking. The restriction to corrected RMSProp is clearly identified.
Ethics: No material research-ethics concern is evident in this theoretical work.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: The AdaGrad results are false as stated. Appendices A.3 and A.6 reuse the AMSGrad proof, but its crucial uniform bound on the accumulated second moment does not hold for AdaGrad. A concrete counterexample to Corollary 5.7 is the 1-smooth Huber objective f(x)=x²/2 for |x|≤1 and |x|−1/2 otherwise. Set x1=4, d=G_inf=L=epsilon=1, s=1/2, T=10,000, and alpha=0.01. Every iterate remains above 2, so the average squared gradient equals 1, whereas the claimed upper bound is 0.1304. All stated assumptions hold. The deterministic specialization of Corollary 6.6 fails similarly. This requires a new analysis, not merely additional explanation.

Soundness: The AMSGrad proof also contains incorrect inequalities. Algorithm 1 defines Vhat=diag(vhat+epsilon), so Lemma A.1 supports Vhat^(-1/2)≥I/sqrt(G_inf²+epsilon), not I/G_inf as used in (A.14). Equation (A.13) additionally assumes the normalized initial gradient has infinity norm at most 1, although it can approach 1/sqrt(1−beta2). These errors affect the explicit constants in both expectation and high-probability results.

Significance and limitations: Remarks 5.5 and 6.4 do not establish an advantage over SGD under comparable assumptions. If SGD's gradients satisfy the same cumulative-growth condition, its standard descent inequality yields an optimized O(sqrt(d)/T^(1−s)) bound, at least as fast as the reported exponent. Furthermore, coordinate sparsity with a fixed nonzero activation frequency generally still gives s=1/2; sparsity alone does not imply s<1/2. The manuscript needs a common problem-class comparison, conditions ensuring the stronger growth assumption, and discussion of selecting the learning rate without knowing s.

Originality: The algorithms and principal proof devices are established methods. Novelty therefore rests on the improved guarantees, whose central claims have the problems above. Moreover, comparisons and references stop in 2020, leaving the claims of priority and significance insufficiently established for ICML 2026.

Presentation and reproducibility: Equation (1.1) uses sqrt(vhat)+epsilon, whereas the algorithms use sqrt(vhat+epsilon). Undefined parameters p and q appear in (7.8) and (A.18). These inconsistencies hinder auditing and reproducing the mathematical guarantees.
